Buildings and carts wear down over time. Lost integrity means lost {B_PARAM_VAL_C}value{##}. Since your {CHAR_WEA_C}wealth{##} is measured by what you own, every crack and splinter lowers it.
Time is a patient vandal. Buildings slowly lose {B_HP_C}integrity{##} as the years pass.
Carts, however, suffer from use. The more often they travel, the more they wear down.
Some effects can make your buildings and carts more durable — or more fragile. Still, the safest choice is to buy {B_HP_MAX_C}sturdy{##} things to begin with.
Not all things are built alike. Maximum Integrity determines how much {B_HP_DEC_C}damage{##} a building or cart can endure before it fully deteriorates.
The higher the Maximum Integrity, the longer it takes to wear down completely, provided it is kept in good condition.
Higher-level buildings usually have higher Maximum Integrity.

The final value shown here is an estimate. The actual value for any purchase made from your building will take into account the specifics of the buyer in addition to all other factors influencing the sell price.
Higher {B_PARAM_ATT_C}customer appeal{##} draws more buyers, making items more expensive.
Every buyer brings something to the bargaining table: skill, reputation, a charming smile, or a face the seller simply does not trust. It can all affect the price.
When buying, prices are slightly higher than the market would pay.

The business doing the buying brings its own advantages and disadvantages to the deal. Its reputation, improvements, working conditions, or whatever is currently going wrong behind the counter can affect the price.
The city levies a modest fee off of each transaction for your privilege of doing business at the marketplace. Some refer to it as a protection fee and claim the Robber Baron offers better service.
A lot can change in a year. A good harvest may fill the granaries, a growing city may empty them again, and yesterday's rarity may become tomorrow's common good. Prices change with the times.
The amount of an item sitting in this building affects its price too. A full stock means lower prices, while running low makes every remaining piece more valuable.
The more of an item there is around the city, the less people are willing to pay for it. Scarce goods, on the other hand, can fetch a much better price.
Some goods fill every market stall in one season and are nowhere to be found in the next. People's needs change with the seasons too, and merchants know well enough to adjust their prices.
Every seller has their own way of doing business. Skill and reputation help, but so can a charming smile, a foul mood, or an inexplicable grudge against your hat. It can all affect the price.
When selling, prices are slightly lower than the market would ask.
The business doing the selling matters too. Its reputation, improvements, working conditions, and the occasional bit of chaos on the premises can all find their way into the price.
{S_NEG_C}Negotiation{##} can shift prices in your favor — securing discounts when buying or better offers when selling.
Prices at the {B_STOFRO_C}storefront{##} are often lower than those at the {B_PUB_MKT_C}marketplace{##}.
The service is so good that customers willingly pay a little extra when buying directly from you. This bonus is calculated as a percentage of the {B_PARAM_STOREV_C}selling price{##}.

Fresh bread is in high demand in the morning, while ale becomes more popular after a long day's work. Near the end of the day, even a stubborn merchant might lower the price rather than haul their wares back home. Prices can change quite a bit from dawn to dusk.

Requests, permits, titles, and other official services that keep city officials busy often come with a fee. Whether handled at the town hall or elsewhere, the money is meant to find its way into the city treasury — assuming, of course, the good principles of everyone involved.
When the city has more goods than it needs, the excess can be sold beyond its borders instead of left gathering dust. The proceeds are added to the city treasury.
City officials use funds from the treasury to build, repair, and improve the city. At least, that is what the money is supposed to be for.

This is money the city pays because of the result of an official action, not the cost of carrying it out. Once the matter is resolved, rewards, compensation, reimbursements, and similar payouts may be taken from the city treasury.
When the city runs short of goods needed by its markets and storehouses, more are purchased from beyond the region to replenish local stocks. The cost is paid from the city treasury.
